title: THE FOOD ON YOUR PLATE COULD BE REVEALING SOMETHING ABOUT YOUR FAITH—BUT NOT WHAT YOU THINK
paragraphs: THE FOOD ON YOUR PLATE COULD BE REVEALING SOMETHING ABOUT YOUR FAITH—BUT NOT WHAT YOU THINK

Should Christians Still Obey the Old Testament Dietary Laws? What Jesus, Moses, Peter, and Paul Actually Taught—and Why Getting This Wrong Could Turn a Gift of Grace Into a Burden God Never Asked You to Carry.
There is a Christian somewhere right now who loves Jesus with all their heart… but is terrified that the food they ate yesterday might have offended God.
Maybe it was pork at a family gathering.
Maybe it was shrimp at a restaurant.
Maybe someone sent them a video claiming that eating unclean animals is rebellion against the commandments of the Almighty.
And suddenly, something that once seemed ordinary becomes a spiritual crisis.
What if I've been sinning without knowing it?
What if my pastor never told me the whole truth?
What if Jesus expects me to follow dietary laws that my church has ignored for generations?
And perhaps the most frightening question of all…
What if I think I'm walking in grace, but I'm actually living in disobedience?
If you've ever wrestled with those questions, stay with me.
Because this conversation is not ultimately about bacon, shrimp, or what ends up on your dinner table.
It's about the cross.
It's about the covenant.
It's about whether Jesus Christ truly accomplished what He came to accomplish.

And somewhere between the laws given to Israel, the words spoken by Jesus, and the blood shed at Calvary, there is a truth that can either liberate your conscience or expose the religious pride you've been carrying without realizing it.
But we cannot discover that truth by grabbing one Bible verse and ignoring the rest.
We must allow Scripture to speak in its own context.
Even when it challenges what we have always believed.
Even when it confronts what we have been taught.
And especially when it exposes how easily we confuse personal conviction with the commandments of God.
Imagine standing among the Israelites thousands of years ago.

The wilderness stretches endlessly before you. The memory of Egyptian slavery is still painfully fresh. Your people have witnessed the sea part, the power of Pharaoh collapse, and the presence of God descend upon Mount Sinai.
You are no longer slaves.
You are a people rescued by God.
And now the Lord is teaching you what it means to live as His covenant nation.
Among His instructions are commands concerning food.

Leviticus 11 distinguishes between animals Israel may eat and animals Israel must avoid. Land animals generally must both chew the cud and have divided hooves. Creatures living in water must have fins and scales.
And then comes the command concerning the pig.
Leviticus 11:7–8 identifies the swine as unclean for Israel because it has divided hooves but does not chew the cud. Israel is forbidden to eat its flesh.
This was not an invention of religious leaders.
It was not a cultural preference disguised as Scripture.
It was a genuine commandment given by God under the Mosaic covenant.
And that matters.
Because anyone who teaches that the Old Testament dietary laws were never commanded by God is already mishandling the Bible.
But there is another question we must ask.
To whom was this command given, under which covenant, and how does the coming of Jesus Christ affect its application today?
That is where the discussion becomes more profound.
In Leviticus 11:44, God declares:
"For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy."
The Hebrew word for holy is קָדוֹשׁ (qādôsh), carrying the sense of holiness, sacredness, and being set apart.
Israel's food distinctions were part of a much larger covenant system that shaped the nation's worship, identity, and separation from surrounding peoples.
The dietary commands were not merely about nutrition.
They belonged to Israel's holy calling under the law of Moses.
Leviticus 20:25–26 connects the distinction between clean and unclean animals with God's separation of Israel from the nations.
And here is something we must not miss.
Israel did not earn its rescue from Egypt by first obeying dietary laws.
God delivered His people, and then He gave them covenant instructions.
Redemption came before Sinai.
Yet the commandments given at Sinai were real obligations for those living under that covenant.
So when someone says, "God commanded His people not to eat pork," they are quoting a genuine biblical reality.
But when someone immediately concludes, "Therefore every Christian must obey the same dietary restrictions today," they have made a theological leap that must be examined through the New Testament.
Because something happened after Sinai.
Something the prophets anticipated.
Something the apostles proclaimed.
Something that changed the history of redemption forever.
Jesus came.
And He did not come merely to give Israel another collection of religious instructions.
He came to fulfill the Scriptures.
In Matthew 5:17, Jesus declares:
"Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil."
The Greek verb translated "fulfil" is πληρῶσαι (plērōsai), from plēroō, meaning to fulfill, complete, or bring to fullness.
Jesus was not announcing that God's previous revelation had been a mistake.
He was declaring that His mission brought the law and the prophets toward their intended fulfillment.
But notice something important.
Fulfillment does not mean that every commandment continues to function in precisely the same covenantal way.
Christians do not continue offering animal sacrifices at the Jerusalem temple.
We do not seek forgiveness through the Levitical priesthood.
We do not regard circumcision as a requirement for belonging to God's covenant people.
Why?
Because the New Testament teaches that Christ's sacrifice, priesthood, and covenant work have transformed how God's people relate to those institutions.
Hebrews 10:1–14 explains that the repeated sacrifices of the law could never perfect worshipers, but Christ offered Himself once for all.
Hebrews 8:6–13 presents Jesus as mediator of a better covenant and describes the former covenant as becoming obsolete.
This does not mean God's holiness disappeared.
It means that God's redemptive plan reached its decisive fulfillment in His Son.
And that brings us to a moment in the ministry of Jesus that should make every Christian pay close attention.
In Mark 7, the Pharisees and scribes confront Jesus because some of His disciples eat with hands considered ceremonially defiled.
The immediate controversy concerns traditional handwashing practices, not a direct dispute over whether pork should be eaten.
That distinction matters.

Jesus rebukes the tendency to elevate human traditions above God's commandments. He then teaches that what enters a person from outside does not defile the heart in the way evil desires and actions do.
Mark 7:20–23 identifies the deeper source of moral defilement: the human heart.
And in Mark 7:19, many modern translations include an explanatory statement that Jesus was declaring all foods clean.
The Greek expression commonly discussed is:
καθαρίζων πάντα τὰ βρώματα
Katharizōn panta ta brōmata.
Literally, the phrase concerns "cleansing all foods."
Many contemporary translators understand it as Mark's explanation of the implications of Jesus' teaching: that Jesus declared all foods clean.
Other interpreters argue that the immediate context concerns digestion, ritual washing, and the foods already recognized as edible under Jewish law.
We should acknowledge that interpretive discussion rather than pretending every detail is uncontested.
Nevertheless, the broader New Testament gives us additional evidence that the old covenant food distinctions are not binding requirements for Christians under the new covenant.
And that evidence becomes impossible to ignore when we arrive at a rooftop in Joppa.
The apostle Peter is hungry.
He goes up to pray.
Then he sees something extraordinary.
A vessel resembling a great sheet descends from heaven, containing various animals.
A voice commands him to rise, kill, and eat.
Peter objects.
In Acts 10:14, he says:
"Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean."
Think about that.
Peter had walked with Jesus.
He had heard His teaching.
He had witnessed His death and resurrection.
And yet Peter still resisted eating what he considered unclean.
Then the voice responds in Acts 10:15:
"What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common."
The Greek statement is:
ἃ ὁ θεὸς ἐκαθάρισεν, σὺ μὴ κοίνου
Ha ho Theos ekatharisen, sy mē koinou.
"What God has cleansed, do not call common."
Now here is where careful Bible reading becomes essential.
Peter himself explains the vision's immediate meaning in Acts 10:28.
God had shown him that he must not call any person common or unclean.
The vision prepared Peter to enter the home of Cornelius, a Gentile, and proclaim the Gospel without treating Gentiles as spiritually untouchable.
Therefore, it would be careless to claim that Acts 10 is simply a story about God giving Peter permission to eat pork.
Its central purpose concerns the acceptance of Gentiles.
But it would also be careless to ignore the way God used the imagery of clean and unclean animals to confront Peter's assumptions about covenant boundaries.
The vision belongs to the larger New Testament revelation that Gentiles are welcomed into God's people through faith in Jesus Christ.
Not by first becoming Jews.
Not by earning acceptance through the Mosaic law.
Not by adopting Israel's entire covenant identity.
But through Christ.
And then came a controversy that threatened to divide the early Church.
Some believers insisted that Gentile converts must be circumcised and commanded to keep the law of Moses.
The issue was serious enough to bring the apostles and elders together in Jerusalem.
You can read the account in Acts 15.
Imagine the tension.
Jewish believers had grown up honoring the Torah.
Gentile believers were now receiving the Holy Spirit and coming to faith in the Messiah.
Would they have to adopt the full Mosaic covenant to be accepted as God's people?
Peter spoke of God's grace.
He warned against placing a yoke upon the disciples that Israel itself had not been able to bear.
Then James gave his judgment concerning Gentile believers.
The resulting letter instructed them to abstain from things associated with idols, from blood, from what had been strangled, and from sexual immorality (Acts 15:19–29).
Notice what the council did not do.
It did not command Gentile Christians to observe the complete dietary regulations of Leviticus 11.
It did not declare that eating pork would prevent salvation.
It did not make the Mosaic food distinctions a condition of justification.
At the same time, the council did give certain food-related instructions, so it would be equally inaccurate to say that food behavior never mattered to the early Church.
The precise relationship between those instructions, idolatry, table fellowship, and later Christian practice has been discussed throughout Christian history.
But the central conclusion is clear.
The apostles refused to make full observance of the Mosaic law a requirement for Gentiles to belong to Christ.
And then the apostle Paul takes us even deeper.
In Romans 14, believers disagree about food and religious observances.
Some eat broadly.
Others restrict their diets because of conscience.
Paul does not command every Christian to eat everything.
Neither does he permit believers to condemn one another over disputable food practices.
Romans 14:3 says:
"Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth: for God hath received him."
Read that again.
The one who eats must not despise.
The one who abstains must not judge.
Why?
Because God has received them.
In Romans 14:14, Paul writes:
The Greek word κοινόν (koinon) here refers to something considered common or defiled.
Paul is addressing how believers regard food in relation to conscience and fellowship.
And then comes Romans 14:17:
"For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost."
This does not mean obedience is unimportant.
It means the kingdom of God cannot be reduced to dietary regulations.
And suddenly the conversation is no longer just about food.
It's about how you treat the Christian sitting across from you.
The brother who does not eat pork.
The sister who eats shrimp without hesitation.
The believer whose conscience is troubled.
The believer who has studied the Scriptures and believes these foods are permitted.
Can they sit together at the Lord's table without treating one another as enemies?
Can they love each other without turning dinner into a courtroom?
Can they remember that the blood of Jesus Christ is infinitely more important than the contents of their plates?
Because Paul continues with a warning that should make every one of us examine our hearts.
Romans 14:20 says:
"For meat destroy not the work of God."
Imagine being so determined to win an argument about food that you wound someone Christ died to redeem.
Imagine proving your dietary knowledge while failing to demonstrate Christian love.
Imagine having the correct menu and the wrong spirit.
That is a tragedy.
And it is not the holiness Jesus calls us to pursue.
But perhaps you are still wondering:
Doesn't the Bible say God never changes?
Yes.
Malachi 3:6 declares that the Lord does not change.
But God's unchanging character does not mean every covenant administration remains identical throughout redemptive history.
The same God who commanded animal sacrifices under the Mosaic covenant also provided Jesus Christ as the final and sufficient sacrifice.
The same God who established the Levitical priesthood has appointed Christ as our eternal High Priest.
The same God who separated Israel from the nations has brought believing Jews and Gentiles together in one body through Christ (Ephesians 2:11–22).
God did not become less holy.
His promises were being fulfilled.
And the new covenant does not make sin acceptable.
It makes the saving work of Jesus central.
This distinction is especially important when people quote 1 Peter 1:15–16:
"Be ye holy; for I am holy."
Peter is drawing from the holiness language of Leviticus.
But he does not use it to command the Church to reinstate every dietary distinction of the Mosaic covenant.
Instead, he calls believers to holiness in all their conduct.
That means Christians must still take holiness seriously.
We must repent of sexual immorality, dishonesty, greed, bitterness, idolatry, cruelty, and every other sin Scripture condemns.
Grace does not give us permission to rebel against God.
Titus 2:11–14 teaches that God's grace trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
But holiness must be defined through the revelation of God fulfilled in Jesus Christ, not through selectively importing old covenant regulations while ignoring the covenantal context.
And this brings us to one of the clearest passages on the question.
Colossians 2:16–17 says:
"Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ."
The Greek word translated "shadow" is σκιὰ (skia).
A shadow points beyond itself.
It is not the final substance.
Paul's point is that these observances must be understood in relation to Christ, to whom they point.
And here is a picture I want you to remember.
Imagine waiting years for someone you love to return home.
You have a photograph of them.
You hold it close.
You treasure it.
You look at it when the nights are lonely.
But then, one evening, the door opens.
The person you have been waiting for is standing right in front of you.
Would you turn away from the living person and insist that you must keep staring at the photograph?
Of course not.
The photograph was precious.
But the person is greater.
In a similar way, the Old Testament covenant institutions pointed forward to the fulfillment of God's redemptive promises in Jesus.
We do not dishonor the shadow by rejoicing in the One to whom it pointed.
We honor God's purpose by recognizing Christ.
That is why Paul warns against allowing others to judge believers over food and calendar observances.
Not because God never gave those instructions.
But because Christ has come.
And if you are a Christian who chooses to avoid pork or shellfish, hear this carefully.
You are not wrong simply because you abstain.
There may be personal, cultural, health-related, or religious reasons for your decision.
You may regard abstaining as a way of honoring God with your body.
You may find it spiritually meaningful.
You are free to make that choice in good conscience.
But there is a difference between saying, "I choose not to eat this before the Lord," and saying, "Every Christian who eats this is sinning against God."
The first may be a sincere personal conviction.
The second requires a binding command under the new covenant that the New Testament does not establish.
Likewise, if you believe you are free to eat pork or shellfish, your freedom is not a license for arrogance.
You do not need to mock Christians who abstain.
You do not need to deliberately offend someone's conscience.
You do not need to turn Christian liberty into an excuse for gluttony or disregard for your health.
First Corinthians 10:31 reminds us:
"Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God."
Notice the scope.
Whatever you do.
Eating.
Drinking.
Speaking.
Serving.
Giving.
Living.
All to the glory of God.
That means your relationship with food should reflect gratitude, wisdom, self-control, and love.
But it does not mean every believer must return to the dietary restrictions given to Israel under Moses.
And perhaps the most decisive theological statement comes from the same apostle who once fiercely defended the traditions of his ancestors.
Paul writes in Galatians 2:16 that a person is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.
The Greek word for justification comes from the δικαιόω (dikaioō) word family, referring in this context to being declared righteous or vindicated before God.
And in Ephesians 2:8–9, Paul says:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast."
This is the center of the matter.
You are not made righteous before God by eating the right animal.
You are not justified by avoiding the wrong animal.
You are not cleansed from sin by designing a flawless religious menu.
You are justified through faith in Jesus Christ, whose saving work is sufficient.
And that should humble both sides of this discussion.
Because the Christian who abstains from pork cannot boast that their diet makes them more worthy of salvation.
And the Christian who eats pork cannot boast that their freedom makes them more spiritually mature.
Neither person can stand before God and say, "Look at my plate. This is why You must accept me."
Our only hope is Christ.
His perfect obedience.
His atoning death.
His victorious resurrection.
His grace.
But there is another passage we cannot ignore.

In 1 Timothy 4:1–5, Paul warns about false teaching that includes forbidding marriage and requiring abstinence from foods God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth.
He explains that what God has created is good and is to be received with thanksgiving, being sanctified by God's word and prayer.
The passage does not mean that everything physically edible is automatically wise, safe, or appropriate to consume.
Nor does it mean all food-related restrictions are sinful.
It addresses religious prohibitions that conflict with the truth of God's creation and the Gospel.
The point is not reckless consumption.
It is grateful reception of God's gifts without turning human restrictions into conditions of spiritual acceptance.
Now, some readers may be thinking about Isaiah 66:17, where the prophet speaks of judgment involving people who eat swine's flesh and other abominations.
This is a serious text, and it should not be dismissed.

Isaiah's prophecy addresses rebellion and corrupt worship within its prophetic context, and interpreters differ about how its final-judgment imagery relates to dietary practices in the age of the new covenant.
But Christians must interpret prophetic passages alongside the clearer apostolic teaching about Gentile inclusion, justification, conscience, and food.
We cannot simply quote Isaiah 66, bypass Acts 15, Romans 14, Colossians 2, and the teaching of Jesus, and announce that every pork-eating Christian stands condemned.
That would not be careful biblical interpretation.
It would be selective interpretation.
And the same caution applies to those who quote Mark 7 and then act as though the Old Testament no longer matters.
Every part of Scripture deserves to be read faithfully.
The law reveals God's holiness.
The prophets reveal His promises.
The Gospels reveal the Messiah.
The apostolic writings explain the significance of His death, resurrection, and new covenant.
Together, they lead us toward Christ.
So what is the answer?
Christians are not required to observe the Old Testament clean-and-unclean animal distinctions as binding covenant law in order to obey God or be accepted by Him.
Believers may voluntarily observe dietary restrictions, but they must not make those restrictions a universal condition of salvation or Christian faithfulness.

At the same time, Christians must honor the food-related moral responsibilities that remain relevant under the new covenant, including avoiding idolatry, practicing self-control, caring for others, and refusing to violate their own conscience.
That conclusion is not based on a single isolated verse.
It emerges from the movement of Scripture from Moses to Christ, from Israel's covenant institutions to the new covenant, and from the Jerusalem council to the teaching of the apostles.
But now I want to speak to the person who came into this article afraid.
The person who has been losing sleep because someone told you that eating a certain food means Jesus will reject you.
The person who watched a frightening sermon and began questioning whether your entire Christian life has been a lie.
The person who desperately wants to obey God but no longer knows whom to trust.
Please hear this.
Jesus Christ is not a fragile Savior whose finished work collapses because you ate a piece of bacon.
The cross was not an incomplete transaction waiting for your dietary performance to finish the payment.
When Jesus cried, "It is finished" in John 19:30, He declared the completion of His earthly redemptive mission at the cross.
The Greek word is τετέλεσται (tetelestai), from teleō, meaning to finish, accomplish, or bring to completion.
That word should never be reduced to a slogan that makes obedience irrelevant.
But neither should we treat Christ's sacrifice as though it were insufficient to save those who trust in Him.
He did not come to make salvation possible only for people who can perfectly navigate every disputed religious regulation.
He came to save sinners.

And if you have been trying to earn peace with God through dietary perfection, religious performance, or constant fear of accidentally breaking a rule, the Gospel invites you to place your confidence somewhere infinitely stronger.
In Jesus Christ.
Not in your menu.
Not in your religious résumé.
Not in the approval of people who measure holiness by outward appearances.
In Christ.
And to the person who has been using grace as an excuse to live carelessly, the Gospel speaks to you too.
Freedom in Christ is not freedom from loving God.
It is freedom to serve Him from a transformed heart.
If you celebrate being allowed to eat certain foods but refuse to forgive someone who wounded you, something is wrong.
If you defend Christian liberty while nourishing hatred, lust, greed, or dishonesty, something is wrong.
If you can debate Leviticus for hours but cannot humble yourself enough to apologize to your spouse, your child, or your brother in Christ, something is wrong.
Because the deepest uncleanness Jesus exposed was not hiding inside a particular animal.
It was hiding inside the human heart.
And that is why we all need a Savior.
Not merely better habits.
Not merely better religious knowledge.
Not merely a more disciplined lifestyle.
We need forgiveness.
We need repentance.
We need new hearts.
We need the mercy of God.
And that is exactly what Jesus offers.
The Gospel is not that you were already clean enough for God to accept you.
The Gospel is that Jesus came for sinners who could never cleanse themselves.
He bore our sins.
He died.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds a Savior who is able to save.
Maybe you have spent years carrying religious fear.
Maybe you have spent years judging other Christians.
Maybe you have been secretly proud of how much Scripture you know.
Maybe you have confused winning theological arguments with actually becoming more like Jesus.
This may be the moment to surrender something deeper than a dietary preference.
Your pride.
Your fear.
Your need to prove yourself.
Your tendency to condemn people whom God has welcomed through His Son.
Because at the foot of the cross, the self-righteous and the ashamed stand on the same ground.
Both need mercy.
Both need forgiveness.
Both need Jesus.
And both can be transformed by His grace.
If this has exposed something in your heart, don't hide behind another theological debate.
Be honest before God.
Not as a formula to earn His favor.
Not as proof that you are saved.
But as a simple expression of your desire to follow Him faithfully.

And if you have studied these passages and understand them differently, you are welcome in the conversation too. Share the Scripture and the reasoning behind your view with humility. We can disagree seriously without treating one another as enemies.
Because biblical truth does not need cruelty to defend it.
And Christian love does not require us to abandon biblical truth.
I also want you to think about someone you know.
Perhaps a family member who has been frightened by religious teaching.
A friend who left church because Christians kept fighting over secondary issues.
A believer who has become harsh and judgmental without noticing.
Or someone who thinks Christianity is nothing more than a thousand complicated rules designed to make ordinary people feel guilty.
Not because sharing a post earns spiritual favor.
But because a single Scripture-grounded conversation might help someone examine the Gospel more carefully.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, people who have grown distant from church, and even those who are still searching for the truth.
They do not need to pretend to have everything figured out before they can begin listening to the Word of God.
And if these teachings are helping you grow, I want to extend a deeper invitation.
Gospel Warrior is not meant to be a place where people merely consume inspiring words, react emotionally for a moment, and return unchanged to their old lives.
Our desire is to keep pointing people to the Scriptures, to the cross, to repentance, and to the daily transformation that comes through knowing Jesus Christ.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible to more people, including those who may not have the means to purchase Christian learning materials.
And this is where your partnership can make a meaningful difference.
That distinction matters deeply to us.
God's grace is not for sale.
And your spiritual worth is never measured by what you can afford.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not come from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
So if you choose to partner with us, let it be because you believe in the mission and genuinely desire to help us continue.
Those products are simply another way to encourage faith, share Scripture, and keep meaningful reminders of Christ in everyday life.
It is the opportunity to help make Christ-centered resources available to people who need them.
Somewhere, someone may be reading Scripture for the first time.
Someone may be quietly wrestling with doubt.
Someone may be ashamed to return to church.
Someone may be wondering whether Jesus could possibly forgive what they have done.
We cannot promise what every article, resource, or shared message will accomplish.
But we can faithfully plant seeds, speak the truth, and trust God with the results.
Pray for the ministry.
Encourage someone who needs the Word of God.
Speak about Jesus with kindness and courage.
Those acts of faithfulness matter too.
Because the goal was never to build a community of people who simply agree with every article we publish.
The goal is to point people toward the living Christ.
To help believers open their Bibles.
To encourage honest repentance.
To remind the weary that grace is real.
To proclaim that forgiveness is found in Jesus.
And to show a watching world that biblical truth and genuine love belong together.
Now return with me to the question that brought us here.
Should Christians follow Old Testament dietary laws today?
You have seen that the dietary commands were real, holy-covenant instructions given to Israel.
You have seen that Jesus came not to dismiss God's revelation but to fulfill it.
You have seen that the apostles did not impose the full Mosaic dietary code upon Gentile believers.
You have seen that Paul instructed Christians not to judge or despise one another over food and conscience.
And you have seen that the foundation of our acceptance before God is not what we eat, but Jesus Christ.
So the next time you sit down at a table, remember this.
Give thanks.
Honor your conscience.
Respect your brother or sister.
Exercise wisdom.
Do not use your freedom to wound someone else.
Do not use your convictions to condemn someone whom Christ has received.
And never confuse the outward appearance of religious discipline with the inward transformation of the Holy Spirit.
Because a person can avoid every unclean animal mentioned in Leviticus and still harbor a heart filled with hatred.
And a person can enjoy a meal that would have been forbidden under the Mosaic covenant while walking humbly before God through faith in Jesus Christ.
The food does not save either one.
Christ alone saves.
The real question is not simply whether your plate is clean according to the old covenant dietary code.
The deeper question is whether your heart has been surrendered to the Savior.
Have you repented of your sin?
Are you trusting in Jesus rather than your own righteousness?
Are you growing in love?
Are you becoming more truthful, merciful, patient, and obedient to Christ?
Are you learning to recognize the difference between the commandments of God and the traditions or convictions of human beings?
Because one day, you will not stand before Jesus holding a menu as the evidence that you deserve eternal life.
You will stand before the One who knows every secret of your heart.
And your only sufficient hope will be His mercy.
So don't make food your savior.
Don't make religious performance your righteousness.
Don't make your personal convictions the cross upon which you crucify your brothers and sisters.
Look to Jesus.
The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.
The fulfillment of God's promises.
The mediator of the new covenant.
The risen Lord.
The Savior who does not merely change what is permitted on a plate, but transforms the hearts of those who belong to Him.
And if you remember nothing else from this article, remember this:
The greatest danger was never that you might eat something unclean—it was that you might spend your life trying to make yourself clean while overlooking the only Savior who can wash away your sins.
